title: Reducing Customer Support Costs at QuickKart

scoping.referenceStatement: Reduce QuickKart's support cost by cutting avoidable queries in the highest-volume categories (order tracking, late delivery) through product self-service, while keeping customer satisfaction at or above 3.5/5 within the existing support budget.

keyTerms.why: Cost per query, total agent cost or cost per order? The COO's goal needs a metric.
Which queries can product changes actually remove? Missing/wrong items may need ops fixes, not product.
CSAT on resolved support queries or overall app satisfaction? The 3.5/5 floor needs a definition.
Priority by query volume, cost per query, or impact on satisfaction?

scenario.context:
QuickKart is an Indian quick-commerce platform operating in 25 cities. It delivers groceries and household essentials within 15–30 minutes.

Over the last six months, the business has grown by 40%, but customer support costs have increased by 75%. Customers complain about delayed responses, while support agents are struggling to manage their workload.

The COO wants to reduce support costs without negatively affecting customer satisfaction.

steps.task: You are the PM responsible for customer support experience. Work through each part in order.
taskPoints: Estimate how many support agents QuickKart needs to handle the current query volume.
Identify which query categories should be addressed first.
Map the business objective of reducing support costs to measurable product outcomes.
Recommend product opportunities to reduce avoidable support queries.
Create a prioritised roadmap for the next two quarters.
constraints: Customer satisfaction must not fall below 3.5/5.
The company cannot increase its support budget.
Engineering capacity is limited to two squads.
deliverables: A two-quarter roadmap with success metrics.
hints: Workload in minutes = 480,000 × 6. An agent supplies 160 × 60 × 75% productive minutes.
Order tracking and late delivery together are 55% of volume — and both are tied to the delivery promise.

worksheet.placeholder: Show your arithmetic: workload ÷ productive minutes per agent.

worksheet.placeholder: Where does query volume concentrate, and why there?

worksheet.placeholder: Sequence initiatives across two quarters, with success metrics.

sections.title: 1. Agent requirement
points: Monthly workload = 480,000 queries × 6 minutes = 2.88 million minutes.
Productive time per agent = 160 × 60 × 75% = 7,200 minutes.
Agents required = 2,880,000 ÷ 7,200 = 400 agents.
With a 10% buffer: approximately 440 agents.

sections.title: 2. Priority query categories
points: Order tracking (30%) and late delivery (25%) should be prioritised as they contribute 55% of all queries.

sections.title: 3. Product outcomes
points: Reduce support queries per 1,000 orders.

Improve first-contact resolution.
Maintain or improve customer satisfaction.

points: Real-time order tracking.
Proactive delivery delay notifications.
Self-service refunds.
Easy reporting of missing or incorrect items.

sections.title: 5. Roadmap
points: Prioritise order tracking, followed by proactive notifications and self-service issue resolution.
Measure the reduction in support queries alongside customer satisfaction.

rubric: A two-quarter roadmap with success metrics.

title: Finding the Right Customers for a Subscription Business — FitLife

scoping.referenceStatement: Prioritise fitness enthusiasts and working professionals, and raise their LTV by improving first-week activation (three workouts) rather than acquiring more low-conversion beginner users.

keyTerms.why: Value by current revenue, LTV potential, or market size? The CEO and Growth Lead read it differently.
Wrong for the product, or underserved by activation? The data supports either story.
Three workouts in week one is an observed correlation, not a proven causal habit metric.
Grow conversion, retention, or LTV — each implies a different intervention.

scenario.context:
FitLife is a fitness app offering personalised workout plans, diet tracking and live sessions with fitness coaches.

The app has acquired 500,000 users in the last year. However, only 8% of users convert to a paid subscription, and monthly churn among paid users has reached 12%.

The CEO believes the company is attracting the wrong customers and wants the product team to identify its highest-value segments.

notes.title: Additional observations
items: 70% of users who complete three workouts in their first week remain active after 30 days.
Only 18% of new users complete three workouts in their first week.
Users who attend at least one live coaching session have 30% higher subscription renewal.
Paid acquisition accounts for 65% of new users.
The average CAC is ₹350.
Monthly subscription price is ₹499.

notes.title: Internal perspectives
items: CEO: "We should focus on fitness enthusiasts. They are more likely to pay."
Growth Lead: "Beginners are a much larger market. We should improve conversion through discounts."
Head of Product: "Perhaps the real issue is that users never develop a workout habit."

steps.task: Work through each part in order.
taskPoints: Identify the most attractive customer segments. Consider both current value and growth potential.
Explain which segments should be prioritised and which should be deprioritised.
Design a research plan to understand why users fail to develop a workout habit.
Identify the key activation behaviours that could predict long-term retention.
Recommend product and acquisition experiments to improve LTV.
deliverables: Research plan with interview participants and questions.
hints: Compare conversion × churn per segment, and weight by share of users.
70% of users who finish three workouts in week one stay past day 30 — only 18% do.

title: The Referral Program That Isn't Growing — PlayZone

title: Should We Launch a Premium Plan? — Streamly

scoping.referenceStatement: Pilot a ₹149 premium tier (ad-free, offline, exclusives) for heavy Streamly users, and expand only if incremental subscription revenue exceeds cannibalised ad revenue and added content cost.

keyTerms.why: Which bundle — all three benefits or a subset? Each has a different cost and willingness to pay.
Stated demand is not willingness to pay; only a pilot or price test shows that.
Defined by 90 min/day — but is the segment big enough to hit the profit bar?
Profitable per subscriber, or after content cost and lost ad revenue from upgraders?

Its current business model relies on advertising and a basic subscription plan costing ₹99 per month.

title: The A/B Test That Misled Everyone — ShopEase

scoping.referenceStatement: Hold the new checkout until it shows a significant lift in revenue per visitor on both platforms, outside sale effects, without worsening payment failures, refunds or support contacts.

keyTerms.why: Completion is up, but AOV, failures, refunds and support contacts all moved the wrong way.
Roll out to all users, Android only, or iterate first? The platform split matters.
The analytics team has not run the test — a 4-point lift could still be noise or a sale-event effect.
Better for completion rate, or better for revenue per visitor? The decision flips on this.

scenario.context:
ShopEase is an e-commerce platform with 5 million monthly active users.

The product team recently tested a redesigned checkout experience. The new version reduces the number of checkout steps and introduces a prominent one-click purchase button.

The initial results look promising. The Head of Growth wants to roll out the new checkout to all users immediately.

However, the analytics team has raised concerns.

notes.title: Additional information
items: The new checkout was tested on both Android and iOS.
Android users showed a 7 percentage-point increase in checkout completion.
iOS users showed no meaningful change.
The test ran during a major sale event.
The analytics team has not yet checked statistical significance.

hints: Check direction on every metric: completion up, but AOV, failures, refunds and support contacts all worsened.

title: The AI Assistant That Users Don't Trust — HelpMate

title: The Product Launch That Nobody Noticed — NoteFlow

scoping.referenceStatement: Fix AI summary quality, recording setup and privacy communication to lift 7-day repeat usage for meeting-heavy professionals, before spending more on awareness marketing.

keyTerms.why: Is adoption trials, completed summaries, or 7-day repeat usage? They fail at different stages.
Against what target? 900 of 6,000 triers returned — retention, not awareness, is broken.
Which users? Existing heavy users say they already have other tools — positioning is unclear.
60% of triers found the output weak — more spend would pour users into a leaky funnel.

scenario.context:
NoteFlow is a productivity app that helps professionals organise meeting notes, tasks and project updates.

The company recently launched an AI meeting summarisation feature after spending three months building it.

The launch received positive feedback internally, and the marketing team ran a campaign across social media, email and the website.

However, adoption has been disappointing.

Users who used it again within 7 days

notes.title: Additional findings
items: 60% of users who tried the feature said the output required too much editing.
25% did not understand how to connect their meeting recordings.
15% were concerned about meeting privacy.
Existing users say they already use other tools for meeting summaries.
The marketing team wants to increase campaign spending.

steps.task: Work through each part in order.
taskPoints: Diagnose where the launch funnel is breaking down.
Determine whether this is an awareness, activation, usability, value or positioning problem.
Identify the most promising target segment.
Recommend changes to the product experience and launch strategy.
Decide whether additional marketing investment is justified.
Define the metrics for a relaunch.
hints: 700k saw it, 6k tried, 900 returned — the break is after first use, not awareness.
60% cite editing effort; 25% can't connect recordings — fix activation before spending on media.

title: A Critical Feature Is Causing More Harm Than Good — RideNow

scoping.referenceStatement: Roll back the automatic allocator where harm is concentrated, restore completed rides and driver satisfaction to baseline, and relaunch only against explicit relaunch criteria (cancellations, rejections, complaints).

keyTerms.why: Which metric defines harm — cancellations, driver satisfaction, or the 6% drop in completed rides?
No distance threshold is defined; 'near' in the algorithm is not 'acceptable' to drivers.
What does fixed mean — the 6-week redesign, or interim mitigations with a relaunch bar?
A deadline is not a success metric; relaunch needs measurable criteria.

scenario.context:
RideNow is a ride-hailing platform operating in 15 Indian cities.

The company recently launched an automatic driver allocation feature designed to reduce passenger waiting times.

The feature uses an algorithm to assign nearby drivers to ride requests.

Initially, the launch appeared successful. Average driver allocation time decreased significantly.

However, within two weeks, the company started receiving complaints from drivers and passengers.

notes.title: Additional findings
items: Drivers complain that some allocated rides are too far away.
Passengers report that drivers accept and then cancel.
The algorithm prioritises the nearest driver, without considering driver preferences or traffic.
The engineering team says a full redesign will take six weeks.
The CEO wants the feature fixed before the next city expansion.

steps.task: Work through each part in order.
taskPoints: Assess the severity and business impact of the issue.
Decide whether to roll back, disable selectively or continue with the feature.
Identify the most important information needed to understand the problem.
Recommend immediate mitigations and longer-term improvements.
Prepare a communication plan for drivers, customers and internal stakeholders.
Define the criteria for safely relaunching the feature.
hints: Allocation got faster, but completed rides fell 6% and driver satisfaction dropped 4.1 → 3.2.
Nearest-driver matching ignores distance, traffic and driver preferences — mitigation can precede the 6-week redesign.

sections.title: 1. Problem diagnosis
points: Driver allocation time has improved, but cancellations, complaints and driver dissatisfaction have increased.
Completed rides have fallen by 6%.

sections.title: 2. Recommendation
points: Temporarily roll back or selectively disable the new allocation logic in affected markets while investigating the issue.

sections.title: 3. Immediate actions
points: Investigate driver rejection and cancellation patterns.
Include traffic and driver preferences in allocation.
Test revised matching logic in a limited market.
Communicate the issue and mitigation to drivers and customers.

sections.title: 4. Relaunch criteria
points: Cancellation rate returns to or below its previous level.
Driver satisfaction recovers.
Completed rides return to baseline or improve.
Passenger complaints decline.

sections.title: 5. Metrics
points: Allocation time, driver acceptance rate, cancellation rate, completed rides and driver satisfaction.

content.consideration: Faster allocation is not a success if it results in fewer completed rides and a worse experience.
